topics.title: The cell and its organelles
topics.notes:
The cell is the basic structural, functional and organizational unit of life. Living systems share general features: a chemical composition built from macromolecules, metabolism, development, reproduction and a relationship with the environment. Breathing is not a general feature, because it belongs only to some animals. The four biological macromolecules are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Glucose is a monosaccharide, so it is a small unit and not a macromolecule. Amino acids are the monomers of proteins. Evolution and inheritance are two of the unifying theories of zoology. The four basic animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue, and "serous" describes a type of secretion, not a tissue.

Organelles and their jobs: the nucleus holds the DNA and is the information center; ribosomes are the protein workbenches; rough ER carries ribosomes while smooth ER makes lipids and steroid hormones; the Golgi body packages and exports; mitochondria are the energy house; lysosomes hold digestive enzymes and act as suicide bags; centrioles are barrel-shaped organelles in animal cells and most protists; polysomes are groups of ribosomes. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum. Food reserves are stored in the cytoplasm. The nucleus is the largest and most easily seen organelle.

Animal cells have centrioles, pinocytotic vesicles, microvilli and lysosomes, but no plastids. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus, their DNA is wrapped around histones, they usually divide by mitosis and they hold more DNA than prokaryotes. A prokaryote keeps its chromosome in the nucleoid region. Chromosomes carry the hereditary material. Mature mammalian red blood cells lose their nuclei.

Histology is the study of the detailed structure of cells and tissues under a microscope. Eosin stains cytoplasm pink and hematoxylin stains nuclei blue. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) was the first to see bacteria and protozoa. The genetic code links the base sequence of DNA/RNA to the amino acid sequence of a protein.

KEY FORMULA: Nucleus = information center;  ribosome = protein workbench;  lysosome = suicide bag;  no plastids in animals

topics.title: Plasma membrane and transport
topics.notes:
The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. Biological membranes are made mainly of lipids and proteins. The membrane is selectively permeable and acts as a gatekeeper for substances going in and out. Myelin is a lipid-rich membrane with about 76% lipid and 18% protein.

Passive transport needs no chemical energy and moves substances down their gradient. It includes simple diffusion, osmosis, filtration and facilitated diffusion. Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated transport using transport proteins embedded in the membrane. Active transport uses ATP and moves substances against the gradient. Endocytosis (bringing material in) and exocytosis (bulk transport out of the cell) are energy-requiring bulk transport.

Microtubules are protein tubes that guide movement inside the cell. A GTP cap at each end stops depolymerization. Kinesins move organelles toward the plus end and dyneins move them toward the center of the cell (the minus end).

KEY FORMULA: Passive = no ATP;  active = ATP;  facilitated diffusion = carrier proteins;  exocytosis = out of the cell
topics.keyFormula: Passive = no ATP;  active = ATP;  facilitated diffusion = carrier proteins;  exocytosis = out of the cell

topics.title: Mitosis, meiosis and the cell cycle
topics.notes:
Interphase comes before mitosis and is not part of mitosis. DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase. Mitosis has four stages: prophase (usually the longest), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator of the spindle), anaphase (chromatids pull apart) and telophase (nuclear membranes re-form). Mitosis gives genetically identical cells and its roles are growth, cell replacement, regeneration and genetic stability. Genetic variation comes from meiosis.

After S phase a human cell still has 46 chromosomes, but each has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere, so there are 92 chromatids. A pair of centrioles is a centrosome.

In meiosis prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and the synaptonemal complex holds them together. A chiasma is the point where non-sister chromatids cross over and swap genetic material. Crossing over takes place in prophase I. In the second meiotic division of oogenesis, a large ootid and a very small second polar body form.

KEY FORMULA: After S phase: 46 chromosomes = 92 chromatids;  crossing over = prophase I
topics.keyFormula: After S phase: 46 chromosomes = 92 chromatids;  crossing over = prophase I

topics.title: DNA and inheritance
topics.notes:
Heredity is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring. DNA is a very long chain of nucleotides, and each nucleotide has a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate and a nitrogenous base. The sugar-phosphate backbone carries the bases. Adenine, cytosine and guanine are only individual bases.

Traits that appear in the F1 generation are dominant and the hidden ones are recessive. Genes on the sex chromosomes are sex-linked. Examples are red-white eye colour in Drosophila, hemophilia and red-green colour blindness. Premature balding is sex-influenced. Height is controlled by many genes and is not sex-linked.

Human somatic cells have 23 pairs (46) of chromosomes. The human skeleton has 206 bones: the axial skeleton has 80 and the appendicular skeleton has 126. Testosterone and estrogen are steroid hormones, while FSH and LH are not.

KEY FORMULA: Humans: 23 pairs = 46;  206 bones = 80 axial + 126 appendicular

topics.title: Gametes, fertilization and embryology
topics.notes:
One primary oocyte gives one functional ovum, while one primary spermatocyte gives four sperm. Oogonia are produced during fetal development. Spermatogenesis is controlled by the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary together, and inhibin from the testis helps to regulate it. A man makes roughly 120 million sperm per day. FSH and LH are gonadotropins, while testosterone and inhibin are not.

Sperm are activated in the female tract by capacitation, which takes a few hours (about 7). After a sperm enters, the cortical reaction raises and thickens the vitelline membrane into the fertilization membrane. After ovulation the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, a temporary endocrine gland that makes progesterone and estrogen.

Cleavage divides the zygote into a ball of cells called the blastula. Yolk-based cleavage types are isolecithal, telolecithal and discoidal, and radial is a pattern based on the plane of division. Eggs with little yolk undergo equal, holoblastic cleavage. Molluscs, annelids, nemerteans and some flatworms show spiral cleavage. Gastrulation turns the blastula into the gastrula.

Triploblastic animals have three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Ectoderm gives the epidermis, nervous system, receptors and nose. Mesoderm gives connective tissue, muscle, the circulatory system and the excretory system. Epithelial tissues can come from all three layers.

KEY FORMULA: 1 oocyte → 1 ovum;  1 spermatocyte → 4 sperm;  blastula → gastrula;  epidermis = ectoderm
topics.keyFormula: 1 oocyte → 1 ovum;  1 spermatocyte → 4 sperm;  blastula → gastrula;  epidermis = ectoderm

topics.title: Epithelial tissue and glands
topics.notes:
Epithelial tissue covers the outside of the body and lines hollow organs. It is cellular, polarized and avascular, rests on a basement membrane (basal lamina) and may have surface modifications such as microvilli, which raise the surface area. Its functions include protection, secretion and reducing friction. Squamous cells are flat, cuboidal cells have a round central nucleus, and columnar cells have an oval nucleus near the base. Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestine. Stratified squamous epithelium lines the mouth, oesophagus and vagina. Goblet cells are single mucus-secreting cells among columnar cells.

Exocrine glands release their products through a duct, while endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the tissue fluid and blood. Gland epithelium secretes enzymes, hormones and lubricating fluids. Merocrine glands release products by exocytosis and the cell stays intact (salivary glands). Apocrine glands pinch off part of the cell with the secretion (mammary glands, apocrine sweat glands in the armpit and genital area, which give pheromonal body odour). Holocrine glands release the whole cell as it breaks down (sebaceous and Meibomian glands). Ceruminous glands in the ear make earwax. The crypts of Lieberkühn are simple straight tubular glands. "Acinar" describes gland shape, not secretion type.

Serous cells make watery, enzyme-rich secretions. They have round nuclei in the central area and a basal region that stains strongly with basic dyes because it holds rough ER and free ribosomes. Mucous cells have flattened nuclei pushed to the base. The sublingual glands are mainly mucous, while the parotid glands and pancreas are mainly serous.

KEY FORMULA: Merocrine = exocytosis;  apocrine = tip lost;  holocrine = whole cell lost (sebaceous)
topics.keyFormula: Merocrine = exocytosis;  apocrine = tip lost;  holocrine = whole cell lost (sebaceous)

topics.title: Connective tissue
topics.notes:
Connective tissue has cells in an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers. The most common resident cell is the fibroblast. Adipocytes are fixed (resident) cells, and they secrete leptin, which gives feedback about fat stores and reduces appetite. Macrophages arise from monocytes. Bone, cartilage, blood and fat are connective tissues. Cartilage has collagen fibers in a firm chondrin matrix.

Collagen is the main structural protein of the dermis, and it gives tensile strength. Type I forms coarse fibers and Type IV is the key collagen of the basal lamina. Dense irregular connective tissue forms the reticular dermis, and the ligamentum flavum is dense elastic connective tissue. Partly movable cartilaginous joints are found between the vertebrae.

KEY FORMULA: Matrix = ground substance + fibers;  collagen = strength;  Type I coarse, Type IV basal lamina
topics.keyFormula: Matrix = ground substance + fibers;  collagen = strength;  Type I coarse, Type IV basal lamina

topics.title: Muscle, nerve and skeleton
topics.notes:
Muscle and nervous tissues are excitable. Skeletal muscle fibers are built from sarcomeres, the repeating units of actin and myosin. When a muscle contracts the H zone shortens and the Z-lines move closer. Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary, and smooth muscle forms the wall of the stomach and intestine. Purkinje fibers are found in the heart.

Motor neurons are multipolar and carry impulses from the CNS to effector organs. Neurons connect to each other at synapses. The epineurium is a sheath of dense connective tissue around a whole peripheral nerve. Merkel cells in the skin detect touch.

A hydrostatic skeleton uses fluid pressure and is found in sea anemones and worms such as the earthworm (Lumbricus). The sea anemone has circular muscle in the inner layer and longitudinal muscle in the outer layer. A spider combines an exoskeleton with hydraulic pressure for movement.

KEY FORMULA: Sarcomere = actin + myosin;  motor neuron = multipolar;  hydrostatic skeleton = worms and anemones

topics.title: The skin
topics.notes:
The skin has an epidermis, a dermis and a subcutaneous layer (hypodermis). The epidermis comes from ectoderm, and most of its cells are keratinocytes. Hair, hooves and nails are made from epidermal cells. The epidermis is anchored to the dermis by the basement membrane. The dermis is mainly collagen. The lunula is the half-moon at the base of the nail.

KEY FORMULA: Epidermis = ectoderm, keratinocytes;  dermis = collagen

topics.title: Digestion and nutrition
topics.notes:
The main classes of digestive enzyme are proteases, carbohydrases and lipases. Amylases digest starch. Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where HCl activates pepsinogen and provides the acid environment pepsin needs. Ghrelin from the stomach and upper intestine stimulates appetite when the stomach is empty, while CCK and peptide YY reduce appetite after a meal.

Riboflavin is vitamin B2 and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is water-soluble. Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause glossitis, while beriberi is a B1 deficiency. Trace elements such as zinc, iron, iodine and copper are needed in tiny amounts, but magnesium is a macromineral.

Microphagous feeders eat small particles, as the acorn worm does. Amoeba and Paramecium digest food inside food vacuoles, while snakes digest in a gut cavity. In ruminants, chewed cud passes through the reticular groove to the omasum and bypasses the reticulum. Platelets are the smallest of the blood cells listed in the exam.

KEY FORMULA: Protease = protein;  amylase = starch;  ghrelin = hunger;  rickets (child) / osteomalacia (adult)
